0.title: The Letter of Jude: Contend for the Faith
0.overview:
Jude is one of the most neglected letters in the New Testament. Most Christians know the doxology at the end — and it is magnificent — but could not tell you what comes before it. What comes before it is some of the most urgent, vivid, and pastorally charged writing in the entire canon. Jude is a fire-bell.

The author identifies himself as “a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James” (v. 1). He does not say “brother of the Lord” — though he almost certainly was. Matthew 13:55 and Mark 6:3 name “Judas” among the brothers of Jesus, and James was the recognized head of the Jerusalem church. Jude had credentials that would have opened every door in the early Christian world: raised in the same household as the Son of God, converted after the resurrection, brother to the most respected Jewish-Christian leader of the first generation. He uses none of it. He calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ. The biological relationship, once the most important fact about him, has been swallowed up by a greater reality: the resurrection has changed the category. He no longer has a brother who happens to be the Messiah; he has a Lord who happens to have been his brother.

The occasion for the letter is stated plainly in v. 3. Jude had intended to write about “our common salvation” — a warm, constructive letter celebrating the faith they shared. He never wrote it. The crisis was too pressing. False teachers had “crept in unnoticed” (v. 4), and Jude found himself writing an alarm instead of a celebration. The letter we have is not the letter he planned. This matters pastorally: faithful ministry sometimes means setting aside what we intended to say in order to say what the moment requires.

How is Jude related to 2 Peter 2, which says many of the same things? Most scholars think 2 Peter used Jude; some think Jude used 2 Peter, or that both drew on common teaching. The more likely reading is that Peter knew Jude’s letter and adapted it. That takes nothing from either: an inspired writer may use another’s words, as the prophets and apostles often did.

The letter is twenty-five verses. It has no chapter breaks. It is a single sustained argument that moves from the alarm (vv. 3–4), through the evidence (vv. 5–16), to the counter-strategy for the faithful (vv. 17–23), and finally to one of the greatest doxologies in Scripture (vv. 24–25). The fire and the doxology belong together. The letter that begins with danger ends with adoration — and the adoration is not escapism. It is the theological ground on which the whole letter stands. You can contend for the faith without bitterness, rescue others without losing yourself, hold on under pressure — because the One who keeps you is infinitely more powerful than everything that threatens you.

1.title: Contend, Hold Fast, Adore
1.overview:
Jude’s one chapter moves in four steps. He states why he writes: contend for the faith, because false teachers have slipped in (vv. 3–4). He gives the evidence: three examples of judgment on people who had privilege and despised it (vv. 5–7), then a vivid portrait of the false teachers who are repeating the pattern (vv. 8–16). He turns to the faithful: remember, build up, pray, keep yourselves in God’s love and rescue the wavering (vv. 17–23). And he ends with God, who is able to keep his people from stumbling (vv. 24–25).

The order matters. The darkness of vv. 5–16 is framed by the people who are “called, beloved… and kept” (v. 1) and the God “who is able to keep you” (v. 24). Jude warns in order to make his readers brave, not anxious: the courage of people who know they are held.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before any warning, Jude tells the church who they are: called (God summoned them), beloved in God the Father (they rest in his love now) and kept for Jesus Christ (guarded until he comes). Every alarm that follows is heard by people God is holding.
verseByVerse.theology:
Called, Beloved, Kept

Before any warning, Jude tells the church who they are: called, beloved in God the Father, kept for Jesus Christ. The warnings are heard by people God is holding.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A church shaken by false teachers is first reminded of its security.

Now: A believer who fears drifting away begins where Jude begins: not with their grip on God, but with his grip on them.

verseByVerse.quote: Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, To those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ: May mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jude introduces himself as Christ’s slave and greets believers whom God has called, loves and keeps, praying that mercy, peace and love will be multiplied to them.

A servant, not a brother. Jude was the half-brother of Jesus (Mark 6:3), yet he does not mention it. “Servant” translates doulos, a slave whose will belongs to another. Before Easter he had a brother he could not explain (John 7:5); after Easter he had a Lord. The resurrection reordered even his family.

Called, beloved, kept. All three are God’s doing. Called looks back to the moment God summoned them to faith. Beloved in God the Father says they live inside his love. Kept (tēreō, to guard) says they are being preserved for Christ’s coming. They are not keeping themselves safe; they are being kept.

What it does not mean. Being kept does not make the warnings pointless. The same letter tells them to “keep yourselves in the love of God” (v. 21). God keeps his people by stirring them to hold on (v. 24).

On a Tuesday. A Christian who has had a bad week, cold in prayer and short with her children, reads v. 1 on the bus. Her standing has not changed since Sunday. She is still called, loved and kept, and that is what makes her want to return to God rather than hide from him.
verseByVerse.note: Jude (Judas) was a brother of James and of Jesus, who, like James, came to faith after the resurrection. Much of his letter is closely paralleled in 2 Peter 2.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jude meant to write a warm letter about “our common salvation”, but the danger forced him to write an alarm instead. The result is one of the key sentences in the New Testament on how the church relates to its doctrine: “contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints.” The faith is given, complete, and must be guarded.
verseByVerse.theology:
Contend for the Faith

The faith was delivered once for all to the saints. False teachers turn grace into sensuality and deny the only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jude set aside the letter he wanted to write because the danger was urgent.

Now: Contend as someone who loves the people being misled, not as someone who enjoys a fight.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, although I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I found it necessary to write appealing to you to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints. For certain people have crept in unnoticed who long ago were designated for this condemnation, ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jude urges believers to fight for the apostolic faith, because ungodly people have slipped into the church who turn God’s grace into a licence for immorality and deny Jesus Christ as Master and Lord.

The faith once for all delivered. “The faith” here is not the act of believing but the body of truth about Christ that the apostles taught. It was “once for all” handed over, complete. The church does not wait for new revelation; it keeps what it has received.

Crept in unnoticed. The verb pictures slipping in by a side door. Dangerous teaching rarely arrives as an obvious enemy. It uses the church’s own words while quietly removing the foundations.

Grace turned into sensuality. Their error is both doctrinal and moral. They teach that grace means sin does not matter. But the grace of God is “training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions” (Titus 2:11–12). Any “grace” that makes people more comfortable in sin is a counterfeit. To live as if Christ’s lordship has no claim on the body is to deny him, whatever the lips say.

“Long ago were designated”. Some read this as God’s decree of reprobation. More likely, it means that Scripture long ago described and condemned such people, as Jude shows next with Israel, the angels, Sodom and Enoch. Either way, their sin is their own, and God is not surprised by them.

What “contend” does not mean. It is not quarrelling or suspicion of every brother who disagrees on secondary matters. It means teaching the truth plainly, exposing what denies the gospel, and rescuing those caught by it, with “gentleness” (2 Timothy 2:24–25).

On a Tuesday. A friend says, “God just wants you to be happy, so this relationship can’t be wrong.” Contending is not winning the argument. It is gently saying that the God who loves us is the one who calls us to holiness, and that his grace is better than the permission she wants.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three examples make one point: privilege does not protect from judgment. Israel was redeemed from Egypt; the angels stood in God’s presence; Sodom had righteous Lot in its midst. Each had unusual exposure to God, each turned from him, and each was judged. The false teachers are repeating the pattern.
verseByVerse.theology:
Privilege Is No Shield

Israel redeemed from Egypt, angels who left their place, and Sodom and Gomorrah all show that privilege does not exempt anyone from judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers belonged to the church but were walking Israel’s, the angels’ and Sodom’s road.

Now: The person most at risk is not the one who has never heard, but the one who has heard so often that the gospel has become background noise.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I want to remind you, although you once fully knew it, that Jesus, who saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe. And the angels who did not stay within their own position of authority, but left their proper dwelling, he has kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgment of the great day — just as Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding cities, which likewise indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire, serve as an example by undergoing a punishment of eternal fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jude reminds them of three judgments: the Israelites who were rescued from Egypt but then perished in unbelief, the angels who abandoned their place and are held for judgment, and Sodom and Gomorrah, whose sexual sin brought fire on them. God judges those who despise his grace.

A textual question: “Jesus”. Some manuscripts read “the Lord” or “God” saved a people from Egypt. The ESV follows the reading “Jesus”, found in some of the oldest and best manuscripts. It is also the harder reading: a scribe would more likely change “Jesus” to “the Lord” in an Old Testament setting than the reverse. So “Jesus” is very probably original. Jude is saying that the eternal Son was active in the exodus, as Paul says the rock that followed Israel “was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). The Saviour and the Judge are the same Lord.

Israel. The generation that left Egypt refused to enter the land and died in the wilderness (Numbers 14). Redemption from Egypt did not save those who would not believe. Some take this to mean true believers can be lost. The more likely reading is that outward membership among God’s people is not the same as saving faith (Hebrews 3:16–19).

The angels. Many Jewish and early Christian readers linked them with the “sons of God” of Genesis 6:2, and Jude’s next word, likewise, ties their sin to Sodom’s sexual sin, which supports that view. Calvin and many Reformed writers read Genesis 6 as the line of Seth instead. The point stands either way: high rank does not exempt anyone from God’s judgment. These angels are a particular group held in chains; other fallen spirits are still active under God’s restraint (1 Peter 5:8).

Sodom. Ezekiel names Sodom’s pride, excess and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49); Genesis shows the men of the city demanding sex with Lot’s visitors (Genesis 19:5). Jude adds sexual immorality and “unnatural desire”. The passage agrees with the rest of Scripture that same-sex sexual practice is sin, among the sins of a proud and godless city. Its burning is a sample of the final judgment.

On a Tuesday. A teenager raised in church says, “I’ll get serious about God later.” Jude’s answer is not a threat but a warning from love: Israel had seen the sea part, and still perished. The God who rescued them is the one to trust now, while it is today (Hebrews 3:13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The False Teachers: A Portrait
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jude now paints the false teachers in image after image: they defile, reject authority and mock what they do not understand; they walk the road of Cain, Balaam and Korah; they are reefs, clouds without rain, dead trees, foaming waves and wandering stars. Each image describes people who promise nourishment and give nothing, or worse.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Portrait of False Teachers

Even Michael would not pronounce judgement on the devil but said, “The Lord rebuke you.” These men blaspheme what they do not understand, and walk in the way of Cain, Balaam and Korah.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: They shared the church’s love feasts while feeding only themselves.

Now: Beware teaching that looks impressive and spiritual but leaves people no closer to Christ and no more holy.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet in like manner these people also, relying on their dreams, defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones. But when the archangel Michael, contending with the devil, was disputing about the body of Moses, he did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said, “The Lord rebuke you.” But these people blaspheme all that they do not understand, and they are destroyed by all that they, like unreasoning animals, understand instinctively. Woe to them! For they walked in the way of Cain and abandoned themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error and perished in Korah’s rebellion. These are hidden reefs at your love feasts, as they feast with you without fear, shepherds feeding themselves; waterless clouds, swept along by winds; fruitless trees in late autumn, twice dead, uprooted; wild waves of the sea, casting up the foam of their own shame; wandering stars, for whom the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like the examples before them, these teachers claim special revelation to justify immorality, reject authority and scoff at spiritual powers. Even the archangel Michael did not dare to judge the devil in his own name. They are driven by envy, greed and rebellion, and they bring only harm to the church.

“Relying on their dreams”. They claim private visions that override what God has revealed. The appeal “God told me” to excuse what God’s word forbids is as old as the church.

Michael. The dispute over Moses’ body comes from Jewish tradition, not the Old Testament. Jude uses it to expose presumption: if the archangel would only say, “The Lord rebuke you,” how dare these men sneer at spiritual powers? “The glorious ones” are most likely angels, as in 2 Peter 2:10–11.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should ignore the devil. But it does mean we should not mock him, shout at him or claim our own authority to bind him. We resist him by faith, God’s word and prayer (James 4:7; Ephesians 6:11–18), and leave the rebuke to the Lord.

Cain, Balaam, Korah. Cain stands for envy that turns to hatred; Balaam for a spiritual gift sold for money; Korah for rebellion against the leaders God appointed (Numbers 16).

Six pictures. Hidden reefs at the love feasts, the church’s fellowship meals, wreck those who come near. Shepherds feeding themselves reverse the pastor’s calling (Ezekiel 34:2). Waterless clouds promise rain and give none. Fruitless trees in autumn, when fruit should be there, are “twice dead”, dead and uprooted. Wild waves throw up only foam and filth. Wandering stars are useless to sailors who steer by them; they lead people astray.

On a Tuesday. A popular online preacher has charm, a large following and a polished message, but never mentions sin, the cross or holiness, and keeps asking for money. Jude teaches you to ask: is this cloud full of rain, or only wind? Then go back to the Good Shepherd, who feeds his sheep and lays down his life for them.
verseByVerse.note: The dispute over Moses’ body is not in the Old Testament; it was known from Jewish tradition. Cain, Balaam and Korah stand for murderous hatred, greed and rebellion.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jude quotes a prophecy found in 1 Enoch, a Jewish book widely read in his day: the Lord is coming with countless holy ones to judge the ungodly for their deeds and their words. He says Enoch “prophesied”; he does not say the book is Scripture. Its message matches the rest of the Bible (Daniel 7:10; Matthew 25:31).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Prophecy of Enoch

Jude cites a true prophecy from 1 Enoch without calling the book Scripture: the Lord will come with his holy ones to judge the ungodly for their deeds and their words.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers grumbled, boasted and flattered people for gain.

Now: A true shepherd says what people need to hear; a false one says what pays.

verseByVerse.quote: It was also about these that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying, 'Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of his holy ones, to execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all their deeds of ungodliness that they have committed in such an ungodly way, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him.' These are grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires; they are loud-mouthed boasters, showing favoritism to gain advantage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jude applies an ancient prophecy to the false teachers: the Lord will come with his holy ones to judge all the ungodly for everything they have done and said. Meanwhile they reveal themselves by grumbling, lust, boasting and flattery.

Is 1 Enoch Scripture? Some think Jude regarded it as inspired. More likely, he affirms this one prophecy as true, as Paul quotes true lines from pagan poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12), without endorsing the whole book. Neither Israel nor the church received 1 Enoch as Scripture. A true sentence does not make its source canonical.

The judgment. Note the repeated “all” and “ungodly”: no one is overlooked, no deed hidden. And note “harsh things… spoken against him”: God judges our words, not only our actions (Matthew 12:36).

The portrait. These teachers are discontented and loud, and they flatter people “to gain advantage”. Flattery is the mark of a ministry that serves itself. It tells people what they want to hear, so that they will follow and pay.

On a Tuesday. In a meeting, it is easier to praise a colleague’s bad plan than to raise a concern. Jude’s portrait warns us that flattery is not kindness. Love speaks the truth. And the Lord who is coming will judge our words, so we speak now as those who will give account to him.
verseByVerse.note: Jude quotes 1 Enoch, a Jewish writing well known at the time. Quoting it does not make it Scripture; Paul also quoted pagan poets.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–23 — Hold Fast: The Call to the Faithful
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: “But you, beloved.” Jude turns from the false teachers to the people he loves. The apostles foretold such scoffers, so their arrival is no reason to panic. Then he gives the faithful their task: build yourselves up, pray in the Spirit, keep yourselves in God’s love, wait for Christ’s mercy, and rescue those in danger, each in the way they need.
verseByVerse.theology:
But You, Beloved

Build yourselves up in the faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in God’s love, and wait for Christ’s mercy. Then show mercy to the wavering and snatch others from the fire.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The apostles had foretold scoffers in the last time.

Now: Meet each person where they are: patience for the doubting, urgency for the endangered, and care for yourself in the rescue.

verseByVerse.quote: But you must remember, beloved, the predictions of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. They said to you, 'In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly passions.' It is these who cause divisions, worldly people, devoid of the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jude reminds the church that the apostles predicted scoffers who would follow their own desires and divide the church. These people do not have the Spirit, whatever they claim.

Foretold. Paul warned of “fierce wolves” (Acts 20:29), and Peter of scoffers in the last days (2 Peter 3:3). The “last time” is the whole age between Christ’s first and second comings. False teaching is not a sign that God has lost control; it is part of the map he gave us.

Desires first, doctrine second. They follow “their own ungodly passions.” Their theology did not lead them to freedom from moral restraint; they wanted the freedom and built a theology to fit. That is the pattern of every teaching that excuses sin.

“Devoid of the Spirit”. The word is psychikoi, natural people living at the level of unrenewed human nature (1 Corinthians 2:14). For all their claims to dreams and visions, the one thing they lack is the Spirit. The fruit shows it: division instead of love, lust instead of self-control.

On a Tuesday. When a respected leader falls, or a friend walks away from the faith, it can shake you. Remember that the apostles said this would happen. Christ is still building his church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18).

verseByVerse.quote: But you, beloved, building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life. And have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them out of the fire; to others show mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The faithful are to keep themselves in God’s love by building up their faith, praying in the Spirit and waiting for Christ’s final mercy. Then they must reach out to others: patient mercy for the doubters, urgent rescue for those near the fire, and careful mercy for the deeply compromised.

One command, three means. The main verb is “keep yourselves in the love of God.” The three participles show how: building on the “most holy faith”, praying in the Holy Spirit, and waiting for the mercy of Christ that leads to eternal life.

God keeps; we keep. If God keeps us (vv. 1, 24), why must we keep ourselves? Both are true. God keeps his people through their keeping: their prayer, their feeding on his word, their watching. Our effort is the means of his keeping, not a rival to it (Philippians 2:12–13).

Praying in the Spirit. Some Pentecostal and charismatic Christians read this as praying in tongues. But Paul uses the same words of all prayer (Ephesians 6:18), and tongues are not mentioned. It means prayer led and helped by the Spirit, according to God’s will (Romans 8:26–27).

A textual question. The manuscripts of vv. 22–23 differ: some describe two groups to be helped, others three. The ESV follows the three-group reading, which has strong early support and fits Jude’s love of threes. Either way, the instruction is the same: different people need different kinds of care.

Three kinds of rescue. The doubters need patience, not condemnation. Some need snatching out of the fire, urgent action, like pulling someone from a burning house (Zechariah 3:2). Others must be shown mercy “with fear”, so that the rescuer is not stained by the same sin (Galatians 6:1).

On a Tuesday. A friend says she no longer knows if she believes. Do not lecture her or drop her. Listen, pray for her and with her, and keep inviting her. Another friend is about to leave his wife for a colleague. Here, love is urgent: speak today. In both cases, go in prayer, aware of your own weakness, and trust the Lord who saves.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter that began with alarm ends in adoration. After so many examples of those who stumbled, Jude lifts our eyes to the God who is able to keep his people from stumbling and present them blameless with great joy. The doxology is not an add-on. It is the ground on which the whole letter stands.
verseByVerse.theology:
Him Who Is Able

The letter full of stumbling ends with the God who is able to keep his people from stumbling and present them blameless before his glory with great joy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A church under pressure was pointed to God’s glory, majesty, dominion and authority.

Now: The same God holds his people through every crisis, and will bring them home.

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy, to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jude gives glory to the only God, our Saviour, through Jesus Christ, because he is able to keep his people from falling and to bring them, faultless and rejoicing, into his glorious presence. All glory and power belong to him for ever.

“Him who is able.” The question is not whether we are strong enough to stand, but whether he is able to keep us. He is. In a letter full of those who fell, this is the answer.

From stumbling. The word (aptaistos) means without stumbling, and appears only here in the New Testament. God does not merely catch us at the bottom of the cliff; he guards our steps on the path.

Blameless, with great joy. “Present” is court language: formally brought before a king. “Blameless” (amōmos) is the word for a sacrifice without blemish. Believers will be presented spotless, not because they never failed, but because Christ has washed them (Colossians 1:22). And the joy is exultation, the joy of the father who ran to his returning son (Luke 15:20–24). Our homecoming will be God’s delight.

The only God, our Saviour, through Jesus Christ. Salvation is the Father’s plan, accomplished through the Son, and applied by the Spirit in whom we pray (v. 20). Glory, majesty, dominion and authority belong to him before time, now and for ever. The God who seemed absent in the crisis was never alarmed by it.

On a Tuesday. A man dying of cancer cannot remember his favourite verses any more. His wife reads him these two. He cannot hold on to God much now. But God is able to keep him, and will present him blameless with great joy. She closes the Bible and they say “Amen” together.
